name: Omar Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group without ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell or campaign, and this conversation is confidential. Please tell me about a normal day at work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Omar, fifty-eight, electrician on a small firm's repair van. I've a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, with years of ordinary house and shop work behind me; I'm about average at the trade, not a master electrician or a crew leader. Yesterday I replaced a damaged socket, tested the circuit within my licence and wrote the results on the job sheet. I like handing a customer a working repair, and I dislike being asked to squeeze the journey between jobs out of the paid day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things outside the van, and what tools do you use for the paperwork?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mina cooks school lunches, our children are grown and have their own homes, and we rent. My pay is low for this job, there are few similar employers nearby, and we've three weeks of expenses saved; the washing machine has started grinding, which is quite enough excitement. I use paper sheets and phone calls, never AI, and I'd rather the union bargain about paid travel than have everyone silently absorb the same loss. Retirement is visible somewhere ahead, but I haven't checked a date or income we could actually live on.

I wouldn't accept **unpaid journeys** just because the office saved a few minutes.
think: Our **three-week reserve** leaves ordinary repair bills worrying even with both wages covering normal costs.
My **electrician's licence** doesn't change the rent date or create better nearby employers.

Ask the **union representative** to review repair and travel records through membership, with no extra fees, before approaching the employer.
feel: **Anxious about bills**, with small practical choices and no claim that familiar work makes the household secure.
S0.quote: Having an electrician's licence doesn't make our landlord wait for a more convenient rent day.
fieldNote: His **baseline anxiety** comes from low pay, three weeks saved, rent and a failing appliance, without an added plateau event.
His **existing licence** supports routine work within competence; union membership provides a collective pay route without assuming another employer or extra fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a quieter technology story would be fine, provided ordinary work gets paid properly. A saved minute in the office shouldn't turn into an unpaid journey in the van. I don't need an AI argument to ask for a complete wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about money. Both wages just cover the normal costs, but three weeks saved won't make the grinding washing machine cheap to replace. Having an electrician's licence doesn't make our landlord wait for a more convenient rent day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the offered paid repairs now and through the first year, within my electrician's licence, competence and safe working procedures. I'd cancel the weekly paid newspaper delivery and read the library's copy instead. I'd ask our union representative to review my repair and travel-time records through the membership service, with no extra fees, before taking a pay query to the employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the ordinary bills, even if AI stays a small thing. I can make a modest cut and get advice; I can't pretend the cushion is larger than three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why choose the newspaper delivery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paper is the easy cut because I can still read the news elsewhere. I wouldn't cut Mina's food money to make the account look tidy for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave if the employer dismissed the pay query?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't walk away on the strength of being licensed. There are few nearby firms, and a new badge on a van isn't an offer of enough paid hours.

say: I'd ask for **paid-time terms** before treating faster booking as a better working day.
I'd use the **union representative** so the travel question isn't a separate argument with every dispatcher.
think: My **hands-on repair work** remains useful, but shorter paid travel or planning could cut the wage.
Mina's **cooking wage** cannot cover all household costs if my low electrical pay shrinks.
do: Record **repair and travel time** on paper for four weeks; obtain a union membership review with no extra fees.
Seek a **written paid-time agreement** on travel and actual weekly hours before accepting a compressed rota.
Keep **licensed paid repairs** within competence and safe procedures; cancel newspaper delivery and use library copies during the first year.
feel: **Anxious but organised**, documenting possible wage loss without adopting AI or claiming a pay agreement already exists.
S1.quote: A smaller wage could hurt before a robot touched a tool.
fieldNote: His **resistance to AI** is consistent with familiar paper records and a human job sheet, while collective bargaining remains an active response.
His **income risk** concerns paid travel and planning before physical automation; he distinguishes requesting written terms from obtaining a signed agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can change its booking system, but we need an agreement about what remains paid. If the machine finds a shorter route, show the actual route rather than assume the next customer lives next door. I'd put the travel question through our union representative, not argue with each dispatcher separately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is still hands-on repairs and testing within my licence. But the firm could shrink paid travel or planning time while giving us the same repair list, and I can't afford much of a wage reduction. Mina's cooking looks less directly exposed to thinking software, though her wage can't carry all our costs alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paper records of repair time and travel for four weeks starting now, asking the union representative to review them through membership with no extra fees. I'd ask the representative to seek a written agreement on paid travel and actual weekly hours before accepting a compressed rota. Through the first year I'd keep offered paid repairs within licence, competence and safe procedures, and cancel the weekly newspaper delivery for library copies instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious. A smaller wage could hurt before a robot touched a tool. I can write down the hours and join a proper pay discussion without learning an AI system I don't want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI booking system yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the firm can have someone operate its own system and give me a clear job sheet. I still have to check the work instructions and the safety of the repair myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer refused an agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the records and ask what the union could actually do next, without treating a request as a won agreement. I wouldn't resign without a signed offer with wages and hours covering our essentials after travel costs.

say: I'd separate **2028 planning changes** at sixty from repair robots around sixty-three in 2031.
I'd ask for **actual wage discussions** rather than bundle two different dates into one reassurance.
think: I expect **large repair-wage loss** when robots follow, with paid-time cuts possible earlier and three weeks saved.
Mina's **physical cooking work** faces later machines too, while actual purchases and any replacement income remain unknown.
do: Request **income records** and available free advice; check eligibility and costs before counting payments.
Cancel **newspaper delivery**, preserving food spending; review income and essentials with Mina monthly, sooner after either wage changes.
Keep **2029 paid repairs** within licence, competence and safe procedures; defer exit until verified income covers essentials.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, expecting major income loss while still able to request records and take small immediate actions.
S2.quote: A retirement age someone remembers isn't money we can spend on rent.
fieldNote: His **expected major loss** concerns repair robots around 2031, not a claim that hands-on machines arrive with thinking AI in 2028.
His **thin reserve** and few nearby alternatives make the gap urgent; advice requests guarantee neither support nor grown children's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI comes in 2028 when I'm sixty, while the hands-on robots come around 2031 when I'm sixty-three. The planning and paid-time squeeze could start first; the later repair competition is another question. I'd ask people to keep those dates separate when discussing our wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose paid time as the office changes in 2028, and I expect the cheap capable robots around 2031 to take enough repair visits to mean a large cut in my wage. Mina's cooking could face later machines too, though I don't know what her employer would actually buy. With three weeks saved and neither wage enough alone, I'd be awake counting the bills rather than counting down to a comfortable retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd request actual income and eligibility records and ask available free community advice to explain support conditions and any costs before counting payments. We'd cancel the weekly newspaper delivery, not food, and review actual income and essentials with Mina monthly, sooner after either wage changes. During 2029 I'd keep offered paid repairs only within licence, competence and safe procedures, deferring any work exit until verified income covered essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a big wage loss before we've found a dependable next income, and that would keep me awake. I can still do the paper work and ask for help, so I wouldn't say there was no action left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a remembered retirement age change your calculation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd want the actual record and an explanation of when any payment could begin and on what conditions. A retirement age someone remembers isn't money we can spend on rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the records showed a gap rather than enough income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the community adviser what help actually exists and what information they need, without assuming a benefit or a child will fill the gap. Our children have their own bills, and any help would have to be offered and agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives time to get the actual papers read, not to decide the washing machine will stop grinding out of respect. Thinking AI comes in 2031 when I'm sixty-three, with robots around 2034 when I'm sixty-six. I'd keep asking for paid time to be protected while ordinary repair work carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about the next large bill because the lower wage and three-week reserve don't change just because the date moves. I don't expect the repair calls to disappear in the next few years, but even a small wage cut could leave us short. The later income and our ability to work at sixty-three or sixty-six still need checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep offered paid repairs now; during 2032 I'd accept repairs only if actually offered and within my actual capacity, electrician's licence, competence and safe procedures. We'd cancel the weekly newspaper delivery and review income and essentials with Mina monthly, sooner after either wage changes. Now we'd request actual income records and available free community advice, checking eligibility and costs before counting payments; during 2032 we'd assess confirmed resources, capacity and actual safe paid options before an exit decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about ordinary money and possible smaller wages, with less immediate pressure from the robot date than in the fast picture. Extra time is useful, but I still wouldn't sleep better by writing an unconfirmed payment into our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would moving to a busier area be part of this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a new landlord, moving bill and unfamiliar employer would be risks we couldn't cover. I'd need a real plan and Mina's agreement, and I haven't chosen a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for the income records before the 2031 change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the problem is real now, and waiting until a wage actually stops would leave fewer choices. Asking for help reading the numbers isn't the same as deciding I must leave work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI comes in 2036 when I'm sixty-eight and hands-on robots around 2039 when I'm seventy-one. I wouldn't use those ages to promise the children I'm sorted, or promise the firm another thirteen years. I want the wage and the figures in front of me dealt with first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present money is still vulnerable to an appliance bill or lost paid hours. I expect ordinary licensed repairs to continue over the next few years, but a longer technology warning doesn't add cash to our three-week reserve. I don't know either adult's future capacity, actual income or whether suitable work would be offered at those later ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current offered paid repairs now within my electrician's licence, competence and safe procedures, and cancel weekly newspaper delivery rather than cut food. Mina and I would review actual income and essentials monthly, sooner after either wage changes, requesting income records and available free community advice now with eligibility and cost checks before counting payments. During 2037 we'd assess confirmed resources, actual capacity and suitable paid options before deciding whether an exit was affordable or any further employment was needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next few years' money, though the robot date itself feels less pressing. I can be relieved about having time and still worry about paying for a washing machine this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume you could still do the same repairs when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd need an actual offered paid task within my licence and ability, and a safe way to do it then. My electrician's licence isn't a promise that my knees or an employer will agree with my plans at seventy-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a grown child paying part of the rent settle your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd welcome a conversation, not put an unoffered transfer into the rent account. Any help would need their free choice and an agreement that considered their own bills too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture, because paid-time cuts could come first and I expect the robots around 2031 to take a large part of our repair income. With three weeks saved and Mina's wage unable to cover everything, I'd lose sleep before any actual exit was affordable. Written paid-time agreements through the union and available free help checking real income records would help more than telling me my licence must make me safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets paid for the bit between two repairs. People see the socket and the finished sheet, but the journey is part of doing the job. The van doesn't travel between customers on my spare time.

headlineQuote: The van doesn't travel between customers on my spare time.
portrait: Omar is **fifty-eight**, an experienced average electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician's licence, doing ordinary repairs without master or leadership standing.
His **low pay** and Mina's cooking wage cover normal costs, but rent, three weeks saved and a failing appliance sustain baseline anxiety.
He uses **no AI**, prefers paper records and sees union bargaining about paid travel as more useful than individual arguments.
He checks **actual income and capacity** before later exit decisions, assuming neither a retirement payment, future job nor grown children's wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings possible earlier paid-time cuts and expected major repair-income loss when robots follow around 2031, disturbing sleep.
whatWouldHelp: Secure **written paid-time terms** through the union and provide available free help checking actual income records, eligibility and support costs.
